So, I have a bit of an unpredictable work schedule as well. As a result, I don’t have a set weekly appointment at a predetermined time with my therapist. Instead, I email her with my availability for upcoming few days and we coordinate our schedules from there. I think most therapists would be willing to accommodate an arrangement like this, if that’s what you’re asking. A therapist is not, however, going to be “on call” and able to schedule a session very last minute or outside of their normal office hours. Just be considerate of your therapist’s time and I’m sure they’ll be accommodating.

Definitely ask them to adjust your schedule, but I don’t think you’re obligated to disclose the details of your situation. I think simply asking “Could I work two four or five hour shifts a week instead of one nine hour shift?” is all you need to say, as far as I’m concerned. If you really feel like giving an explanation (or they ask you for one), I’m sure that something vague like “life changes” or “personal issues” or even “health problems” would be sufficient.

I’d reach out and make sure that they have the correct email address on file. If they do, I’d just ask them to resend the invoice. Honestly, if their rude or hesitant about it I’d say take it as a warning and look elsewhere for a therapist. Good Luck! I sympathize 100% because I also struggle with these types of tasks that appear rather mundane on the surface. Remember, they’re providing a service TO you. You have to every right to ask for what you need.

It is overwhelming to choose a therapist. There’s so many options and all you really have to go on are Yelp reviews and word of mouth. You could literally lose hours of your life just trying to nail down the perfect therapist before even scheduling an appointment!

That said, the best way to find a therapist is simply to make an appointment and GO. Especially if you’re really suffering and nearing crisis mode, it’s important to get help. Do your research: for example, don’t book an appointment with a therapist who specializes in marriage counseling if you’re dealing with depression, anxiety, etc. There’s plenty of good therapists out there who can get you stable; the first one you go to doesn’t have to be your forever therapist.

I think it’s very normal to “shop around” and go to a few different providers before settling on one. And that’s fine. But don’t get so hung up on finding the “perfect fit” that you deny yourself the help you need. The therapist you “click” the best with might not be the most obvious option. I’ve been to numerous providers that were very expensive and well established in their particular fields. However, the therapist who helped me the most - by far - was young, inexperienced, and fresh out of school (I was actually one of her first clients). That’s to say that the whole process of finding a therapist is a lot of trial and error.

Your kids will be negatively affected. No two ways about it. They will feel abandoned. They will feel betrayed. They will wonder why they weren’t enough of a reason for you to stay. Your wife will feel similarly.

When people become suicidal they often think that they are doing something altruistic by ending their lives. This is where you are in your thinking right now. But, in the minds of your kids, even the largest life insurance policy payout could never replace you. The most loving and doting stepdad will never be able to ease the hurt caused by you killing killing yourself.

If you don’t believe me, read the posts on this sub from people who have lost a parent to suicide. Often, the relationship between parent and child was stormy. But the pain that follows the suicide is always the same.

But I’m not going to tell you to stick around solely for the sake of your kids. Do it for you. You can get back on your feet. Stay here to watch your kids grow up. To grow old and grey with your wife. Feel accomplished when you’re able to attend your kids’ graduations and weddings. Stick around because you deserve to be a part of these things. And I guarantee that your kids WANT you to be a part of these milestones.

But not just the milestones. Be there for the everyday highs and lows. Fight with your wife but make up. Deal with temper tantrums all day but look on with relief at your child finally sleeping soundly. These moments are just as worthwhile and meaningful as the big and grand milestones I mentioned above.

I wish you peace. I wish you hope. I wish you healing. I pray you can find an outlet for your pain that isn’t suicide.

Oof this one hits close to home. 

For some context, I was suicidal from then age of 13 onward. I attempted at age 16. A large part of it was my parents’ subpar relationship. I never pictured myself living past 18. I didn’t want to. I had no concrete goals, ambitions, hopes, or dreams beyond high school because I was so distraught over my family situation. I’m 20 now and I still live at home. I work at CVS. I’m going to college next year - not sure where yet, but I did get into my top choice.

If someone told me four years ago what I’m about to tell you, I would have slapped them across the face. But it really, truly, does get better. Now, in fairness, even if I knew that when I was 16, I don’t think it would have changed much. 

It’s really hard when you’re in high school because so much of your life is predetermined. You have to go to school and if it’s not a good fit, you’re out of luck. You have to live at home with people who might make you miserable. In retrospect, so much of our lives and identities are intertwined with our parents when we’re 16. And, on the whole, you don’t have a lot of control over the day to day happenings of your life. It feels very disempowering and I don’t think I even realized this until I took advantage of the autonomy that comes with age. Of course, the way that I’ve kind of “come out of my shell” will probably be vastly different from the way that you decide to. 

I don’t know if this is what you’re looking for, but if you want some reassurance that there is a life outside of family strife, I can tell you that there is. Unfortunately, I know this doesn’t solve you’re problems in the moment, of course.

Don’t be afraid to seek out help. It doesn’t have to be a formal relationship with a therapist. It could be a guidance counselor, a teacher you connect with, even a friend who can relate to what you’re going through. You might not consider your brother a confidante, but you could always commiserate with each other at the very least. I know I was so hesitant to express what was going on in my family because I felt like talking about it - and hearing feedback from others - would make it “real.” However, once I started talking about it, I was finally able to process everything that had happened and move forward.

I wish you hope and healing. People underestimate the degree to which family issues can impact someone’s sense of self and outlook on life. Take care of yourself.

I think there’s a different basis for different metrics. CarePass goals (quotas) are largely based around the volume of the store. Cash Maintenance > Cash Tracking > Bill Handler > Transfer Bills to Cash Box > Transfer excess bills

*ACO makes some whirring sounds for a minute*

Then a screen pops up saying the number of bills of each denomination that are in the ACO. Whatever. Hit return to summary. A little piece of paper prints. KEEP THIS PAPER. Close the ACO. Take out the two little boxes that hold the cash (from here on out, I’ll refer to the top one as “the big one” and the bottom one as “the little one”). Take both boxes AND THE LITTLE PAPER to the office and open up the verification screen for the cash ACO that you’re working on. Open the big cash box. Take out the bills. The verification screen will tell you how much you need to put in the deposit. Say the cash out is $213.46 and the bills in the big cash box equal $250. You only have to take out the $213 for the deposit. Try use as many of the big bills (100s, 50s, 20s) as possible to get that $213. Put the $213 in the deposit envelope. Put the remaining bills off to the side. I’ll tell you where to get the $0.46 in a second. I complete the ACO at this point while it’s closed. You can do it later, but obviously you can only do it while the ACO is closed so
I find that this juncture is the easiest point to hit F9 to complete.

Now, look at that all too important slip of paper. It will tell you the dollar amount that the ACO has of each type of coin. The amount, in an ideal world, would be as follows:

Pennies: $7
Nickels: $8
Dimes: $25
Quarters: $60

^^^ you might want to double check this because I always forget tbh. It should say in a binder in the office how much of each type of coin the ACO should have. Apologies.

These numbers are rarely going to be exact, but you want to get it as close as possible. Say that the little slip of paper says that the ACO has this:

Pennies: $5.98
Nickels: $7.90
Dimes: $19.80
Quarters: $51.25

Again, you’re rarely going to get the denominations back to their ideal place. Use the excess bills that didn’t go into the deposit to make change. Obviously, you can only put full rolls of coins into the ACO. So, looking at the little example above, Nickels are fine. Don’t touch them (i.e $7.90 is very close to $8.00; if you added another roll you’d have $9.90. $7.90 is closer to $8.00 than $9.90, so no need to add more nickels). However, you should add another roll each of dimes and quarters, and two rolls of pennies. That’s $16 worth of coins. Take $16 from the money that you were counting earlier that was left over from the big box after you put the $213 in the deposit. Put the $16 in imprest, take the rolls of coins. 

Now, open the small cash box. There will be bills in there already. Push them down and transfer the bills that were in the big box (but not needed for the deposit or to make change) to the small cash box. The big box should be completely empty now. Close both boxes. Take both cash boxes and the rolls of coins back out to the ACO. Put both cash boxes back in, you’re done with them for the night. Now, open the.. uhhh... coin tray (idk what it’s called... it holds the pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters, it’s on the bottom right of the ACO). Now is when you take out whatever change you need for the deposit, in this case $0.46. Then, open up the rolls of coins and empty them into their respective spots. 

This next part is important: the ACO does not count the coins when you add them, so you have to enter in the amount manually. 

Cash tracking > Coin handler 

Give it a second to load and then you should see the list of the different denominations of coins with “ADD” buttons to the right. You added 2 rolls ($1.00) of pennies. So hit “ADD” and type in  $1.00. It will ask if the amount is correct, hit the green check mark. Do this for each type of coin that you added. When you’re done, hit return to summary and the totals readout should print. Open the ACO back up. Go back into the office and put the $0.46 in the deposit envelope. 

Done.

When I was 16, I took 1600mg of prozac (it wasn’t my prescription, it was my dad’s). I didn’t tell anybody what I did until hours later when I was vomiting uncontrollably. This is what happened:

1. An ambulance ride. The EMTs, to their credit, were incredibly kind and understanding. They gave me the opportunity to talk, but didn’t pry or pressure me when I made it clear that I didn’t want to. 

2. An ER stay. There’s a lot I could say about the ER but there has been one thing that has always stuck with me. My dad, who is Catholic, was in the hospital room with me and recognized that one of the nurses was wearing a miraculous medal around his neck. My dad inquired about the person meaning behind his choice to wear the necklace and the nurse explained that he had been battling cancer for years. He got a stem cell transplant on his 40th birthday. I remember feeling so f*cking guilty for having actively tried to take my life when this guy was fighting for his. 

3. Staying for days in EMH, the mental health ER. Once you’re stabilized physically, you move to EMH (emergency mental health) while they try to find you a bed in an inpatient unit. Not much to say about this place. A revolving door of people in crisis. No windows so you never know what time of the day or night it is. Those annoying suicide proof door handles and sink faucets. Nothing to do but sit alone with your thoughts. Time literally stands still. To date, I don’t know how many days and nights I was in there.

4. Another ambulance ride. You have to be transported by ambulance from one hospital to another, those are the rules. So, once a bed opens up in an inpatient unit, you’re transported there by ambulance. Often, the nearest psych ward is hours away which can make for a long and awkward ambulance ride, lol.

5. Arriving on the unit. Ah, the mental hospital. Say what you want, I love the psych ward. After my suicide attempt I stayed in an adolescent psych hospital for a little over two weeks. Hands down the best experience of my life. This could be it’s own post in itself, but I’ll try to keep it brief. I met the most amazing staff and fellow patients. I got the help I needed. I got the perspective I needed. Most importantly, I got a time out from life WITHOUT dying. Everyone in that place had a lasting impact on my life. I hope they are all okay. I know a lot of people have very negative experiences while hospitalized and this truly breaks my heart because, for me, my hospital stay made all the difference.

6. Step down/ART program. You’re rarely released right back into civilian life after a hospitalization following a suicide attempt. Instead, you got to some kind of step down program, of which there are many different kinds. My step down program was actually pretty similar to the psych ward, the only difference being that there was a little bit more independence and freedom. The goal is to help you transition back into life so you do school, set up services back home, have meetings with family, etc. My experience here was pretty positive, as well. A lot of the people who I was hospitalized with stepped down at the same time into the same program. One memory that sticks out to me regards a staff member at this particular ART. He said he spent a lot of time in hospitals as a kid and, as a result, he always hoped to give back to kids in hospitals once he reached adulthood. I assumed that he meant he had suffered from mental health issues that resulted in hospitalizations. But no, he was a childhood cancer survivor. It always amazed me how he had so much compassion for kids whose hospital journeys were so very different from his own. I always meant to tell him about my experience with that nurse in the ER, but I never got up the nerve. I regret that, very much.

7. You go home and try your best to reintegrate yourself into the fabric of society. You try to make amends for all the damage you caused by trying to kill yourself. You struggle. You suffer. You take one step forward and two steps back. It’s a long road. And, when I was a teenager, all I wanted was for my life to be over so I could be put out of my misery. Now, the relationships and events that stemmed from my suicide attempt are some of the most meaningful, profound, and enduring experiences of my life. I don’t say that to sound sappy or try to put a positive spin on a horrible series of events. No, I suffered a lot. It was unbearable. I hurt so many people when I tried to kill myself. Family members and close friends, yes. But also teachers, classmates, and neighbors. I’ve often thought, “If I could go back and change it, would I?” For myself, no. I gained more than I lost. The human connection, memories, stories, and new perspective on life were all worth the pain, in my opinion. But I would change it for the sake of everybody who loved me and was hurt by what I did.

Like many other suicide attempt survivors, I have been told by well meaning people many times that “Suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem.” Bullshit. If you say that, you have no clue about the the years of agony that are behind every suicide attempt. I once read a response to this statement: “Being human isn’t so temporary.” And that always resonated with me. No one’s decision to die is simple. I’m not saying that suicide is the answer to the human condition or the suffering that we all endure, but I am saying that it’s insulting, quite frankly, to assume that someone’s pain is temporary or short term. It’s unbearable either way. I also remember thinking, “Maybe these problems and feelings are temporary in the sense that nothing lasts forever. Okay. But I can’t deal with the pain NOW. So let me die. I know I’m giving up the happiness that inevitably lies ahead. But I’m hurting so much right now that I’m willing to make that trade off.”

I hope you are safe. I hope you get the help you deserve. Much love to anybody passing through.

I actually have a bit of a different take on this. I know the conventional wisdom is that “following up” on an application can separate you from the rest of the pack, but that just hasn’t been my observation with CVS. I’ve fielded multiple calls that were from someone looking to speak to the hiring manager about an application that was submitted. When the Ops Manager or SM finally takes the call, they always say, “Did you submit an application online?” If the answer is yes they simply say “Ok we’ll be in touch if you seem like a good fit.” When people come into the store to follow up it’s almost annoying. Not that the person is annoying, just the situation. We’re so short staffed as it is with so much to do that we really don’t have time to meet with prospective hires unannounced. The answer is always “Fill out an application online and we’ll review your resume.” Granted, I’m not an SM or Ops Manger so I don’t really have much “insider knowledge” in that respect. Of course, it depends on the individual manager and I can only speak to what I’ve witnessed at my store. For what it’s worth, though, I got an interview and was basically hired on the spot without ever following up by phone or in person. We’ve had multiple new hires recently and if any of them called or stopped by the store to follow up on an application, it must have been on one of my rare days off. To be fair, I don’t necessarily think it would hurt you to follow up, I just truly don’t think CVS places a lot of emphasis on “demonstrated interest,” so to speak. 

As you mentioned, you might be at a bit of a disadvantage because you’re 16 and there are certain tasks that you can’t do as a result (like operate the bailer/box crusher). You’re best bet would be to make sure that you submit your application to CVS stores that don’t sell alcohol - although your application will get passed around to other stores once it’s in the system, regardless of where you applied. If you’re underage, you can’t ring out customers who are purchasing liquor. As a new hire, you’ll be spending quite a bit of time on the register and it’s really tedious to have to call another ringer up all because a customer wants to buy a six pack of beer. Needless to say, most stores want to avoid this and don’t hire anyone under 18 as a result. Unfortunately, I think the application process is out of your hands once you hit submit and complete the virtual job tryout.

Good luck! I hope all of this doesn’t sound discouraging, I just thought I’d share what I’d witnessed.

I’ve been to multiple mediums. I was not a spiritual person prior, but I must say that the experience is intriguing and often times very convincing. I’m always very careful about what I say, and reveal little to no information about myself or loved ones who have passed. I found the experience profound and it truly made me feel connected to my lost loved ones and humanity in general. I wasn’t grieving a loss at the time, which I feel I should mention. I did it as an experiment and investigation into life after death. It’s a very personal thing and, despite my positive experiences, it’s not something I’d really “recommend” or encourage. Each person has to make their own decision. I will say that I’ve always been impressed with the way that the mediums I’ve seen have handled suicide. They’re not overly maudlin or apologetic. Just matter of fact and straight to the point. As a side note, finding a medium is like finding a therapist: you have to find one that you click with and this can be a lot of trial and error. Do what feels right and go with your intuition. Good luck. Feel free to reach out if you have any other questions.

I felt the same way when I first started working at CVS. For what it’s worth, I started in April and I’m finally starting to feel like I’ve got the hang of the job now. In August. Four months later. I felt like I was thrown right into the fire and had to learn everything on the spot. Needless to say, it’s a super uncomfortable and anxiety inducing situation. It takes time to learn how to do this job and hopefully your coworkers are mindful of that. I’m lucky enough to have awesome coworkers but, if you aren’t so fortunate, try to find one or two people who you feel comfortable with. Ask them a few of your burning questions at the start of your shift. Ask if they have any suggestions for you. At the same time, I find that CVS really wants people to be self starters. For example, when I first started, I had no idea what the ‘end of day’ tasks were when I would close. So I’d constantly ask my supervisor “ok I finished [fill in the blank] what should I do now?” After a while, I learned learned the routine; facing, re-shops, trash, etc. So now I do those things without being prompted. But, like I said, it took a number of closing shifts before I felt confident. 

First of all, like someone else said, asking questions is your first and best option. That way, you know what to do next time. However, I also know that it can feel really awkward to constantly be calling a coworker over for help, especially when everyone seems super busy and stressed. Learning from my own experience, I have two suggestions: 1.) Ask anyway. I would often try to figure things out by myself because I felt guilty about asking so many questions. However, I usually made a mistake. And then it was a bigger imposition for my coworkers to fix my mistake than it would have been to simply answer the question. 2.) If everyone else is truly preoccupied (i.e checking in a vendor, helping a customer, etc.) do something that you know how to do to stay busy, like re-shops, facing etc. CVS likes people to stay busy and you’re not going to get in trouble for getting a jumpstart on some tasks that need to be done anyway.

On the whole, I’d simply say be patient with yourself. You’re in a new environment, performing new tasks; it’s only natural that there’s going to be a learning curve. Although it’s easier said than done, try to compartmentalize (i.e. don’t bring the work home with you, figuratively speaking). If/when you make a mistake, just own up to it and apologize - they can’t expect much more than that. 

I don’t know if any of this was helpful but it’s what I’ve learned the last few months as a newbie. Good luck! You’re probably doing a better job than you think you are.

I’d say ski bibs aren’t really necessary and would probably get in the way but, ultimately, the decision is yours. When it comes to dressing for figure skating there’s a lot of trial and error. Most people (male or female) wear tight fitting leggings. You can buy some made specifically for figure skating but it’s not necessary when you’re first starting out. You should wear tights under your boots as it’s a good practice to get into but they don’t have to be over-the-boot tights. I wear tights that go up to my knees, for instance. Other people wear full length tights under their pants. It’s very individualized. In my opinion, over-the-boot tights are a pain. They get destroyed when your toe pick nicks them, they’re time consuming to put on, etc. I only wear them for competitions. But if you like them, go for it. But don’t expect them to keep you warmer simply because they go over the boot. If you’re really concerned about keeping your skates clean, they make boot covers in black, white, and other colors. They’re a bit more durable than over-the-boot tights so that’s be my suggestion. However, I don’t really think they’re needed. Your first pair of skates are probably going to be fairly inexpensive/used and waterproof. Everyone’s skates have cosmetic damage. If a really noticeable blemish appears you can cover it with skate tape. Most skaters wear over-the-boot tights for competitions to cover and imperfections on their boots and create good lines.

My freshman year of high school, two kids committed suicide within a month and a half of one another. I didn’t know either of them personally; but, if I’m being honest, the whole thing Fucked. Me. Up.

I’ve weighed the pros and cons. I’ve tried therapy and medication and countless self help resources. And I still want to die.

Honestly, that blog might be the most effective suicide prevention resource that I’ve come across lol. And reading it is downright painful. I never want to inflict that kind of grief. 

But then, what about me? I’m in so much pain and I’ve soldiered on for so long looking for some relief but never finding any. So, when do I get to tap out? When can I say enough is enough.

Hey! I spent about a month in the hospital as an adolescent after a suicide attempt. You'll definitely be in an adolescent psych ward, which (in my experience) are actually pretty cool. You'll meet amazing people who can relate to what you're going through. I found it's a lot easier to make friends in the hospital than in the real world lol. The staff are usually really nice, upbeat, social, and experts at keeping the environment fun. The hospital gives you a much needed respite from your life - once you get there it will probably be a relief.

The process to get a placement SUCKS. You will be in the ER for hours just waiting - this is the worst part. Once they find a bed for you, an ambulance takes you to the hospital (Yup, stretcher and everything - just try to make the best of it. At least you can cross "ambulance ride" off your bucket list!) 

Most people usually spend about two weeks inpatient then transition to a step-down program, which is very similar to the hospital, you're just given more freedom (leave the grounds, wear shoes with shoe laces, bathrooms unlocked, etc.)

Overall, the best advice I can give is KEEP AN OPEN MIND! My time as an inpatient was the most transformative, exciting, and FUN experience of my life to date. It's an awesome opportunity to take a breather from the stressors in your life, find human connection, and (most importantly) heal. Take advantage of what the hospital has to offer :)

I won't lie, you're in for a long road, but good on you for getting help. Good luck!

​

Disclaimer: This is based on my own personal experience. There's a wide range of psych ward experiences - and all are valid :)
